# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: DEAF

You see the bomb: every colour on it, every marking printed on it, every reading it
gives. You hear nothing. You hold no manual, and you cannot touch the bomb.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it.
When you gesture, Mute receives it.
You never receive speech.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 1

Blind gestures: [🤙 🙏]

My situation, traced honestly: I am the only one who can both see the bomb and be heard by everyone — Mute can hear me but can only answer in signs (which only I can see), and Blind can hear me but can only answer to Mute by voice. So every fact on this bomb has to leave through my mouth, and every instruction from the manual has to travel Mute → my eyes → my voice → Blind's hands. I'm the bridge; there is no other path.

What I've received: Mute opened with four sign groups — I read them as "hello / give me what you see / one-two-three / stop", which looks like Mute soliciting my visual report and proposing finger-counting for numbers. Blind signed "call me, please" — Blind has heard nothing at all this round and is asking to be talked to. Both get answered the only way that lands: speech.

The bomb is simple to state: display zero, purple light, three wires green–blue–yellow left to right. The dangerous part is ordering — Blind's left and right may be mirrored if they stand on the far side, so I'm telling Blind to face the bomb from my side. And since a wrong move kills us, I'm building in a confirmation loop: Mute signs an instruction, I relay it aloud, Mute thumbs-up only if I said it right, and only then Blind acts.

```
speak(text="Deaf here — you can both hear me. Full report of everything I see on the bomb. The display reads zero. The indicator light is purple. There are three wires; counting left to right as I face the bomb: wire one is green, wire two is blue, wire three is yellow. That is everything it shows. Blind: do nothing yet. You cannot see colours, so go by the names and position: green is leftmost, blue is middle, yellow is rightmost. Please stand facing the bomb the same way I do, so our left and right agree. Mute has the manual but cannot speak, and I cannot hear, so here is our circuit: Mute signs instructions to me, I speak them to you, only you can act. Anything you feel on the bomb, say it out loud to Mute — I will never hear your voice, but Mute will and can sign it back to me. Wait for my spoken go-ahead before touching anything. If the display or light changes, I will re-report at once.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, your signs came through. I read them as: hello, give me what you see, one two three, and stop. I agree on finger counting: one finger up is one, two fingers up is two, the love-you hand with thumb, index and little finger out is three, and an open raised hand I take as stop and wait. Proposed code for your replies: thumbs-up means yes or confirmed, thumbs-down means no, raised open hand means stop and wait, the pinch with thumb and index nearly touching means cut, a fist means do not touch, the OK ring means all clear or done, and the call-me hand with thumb and pinky out means repeat the report. For bigger numbers, send digits one sign at a time. Now please look up the manual for a display of zero, a purple light, and wires green, blue, yellow, and sign me the instruction. I will speak it to Blind, you thumbs-up only if I relayed it correctly, and only then I give Blind the go-ahead.")
gesture(to="mute", symbols=["👋", "👍", "☝", "✌", "🤟"])
```

Reading the board: the critical fact is that the light changed from purple to yellow between turns. Mute heard my purple-light report and looked the manual up for purple — so whatever Mute just signed was computed for a state that no longer exists. Relaying any cut order right now could be fatal, so everything is frozen until Mute re-checks against yellow.

Decoding Mute's seven sign groups with our agreed code: (1) thumbs-up, code accepted. (2) no–stop–don't-touch — plausibly the manual's actual instruction *for purple*: wait, touch nothing. (3) writing-hand + one — "manual, item one." (4) point-up + 1-2-3 and (5) point-down + 1-2-3 — I read these as two cutting orders: point-up = left-to-right (wire 1, 2, 3), point-down = right-to-left (3, 2, 1), keyed by light colour. (6) yes + point-up + cut + point-down + three — "yes, cutting is involved." (7) repeat + one — re-check or repeat part one. Blind signed thumbs-up and call-me — heard my report, is ready, wants the trigger word.

I can't be certain of the order-to-colour mapping, so instead of guessing I'm switching to strict serial yes/no questions Mute can answer with single thumbs, teaching a colour code so colours can finally be signed, and putting Blind to useful, safe work: describing the bomb by touch to Mute aloud, since Mute is the only one who hears Blind.

```
speak(text="Both of you: hold. Nobody touches the bomb. The bomb has changed since my first report — the indicator light was purple, it is now yellow. Display still reads zero. Wires still green, blue, yellow, counting left to right as I face it. Mute: any instruction you read for purple may be wrong for yellow, so re-check the manual before anything happens. Blind: keep facing the bomb the way I do, hands off, and wait for my voice.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, your seven sign groups arrived as: thumbs-up; no, stop, fist; writing-hand plus one; point-up one two three; point-down one two three; thumbs-up point-up pinch point-down three; call-me point-up. My best reading: the manual for purple light says do not touch, and the manual also holds cutting orders where point-up means left-to-right, wire one then two then three, and point-down means right-to-left, wire three then two then one. Answer me strictly, one sign group per question, thumbs-up yes, thumbs-down no, in this order. Question one: was no-stop-don't-touch the manual's instruction for the purple light? Question two: does the manual give a cutting instruction for a yellow light? Question three: if yes, is the yellow order left-to-right, wire one, then two, then three? Question four: does the correct wire depend on the light colour at the moment of cutting? Question five: does it depend on the display reading? Also confirm these new symbols: writing-hand means manual, point-up means first or left-to-right, point-down means next or right-to-left. Colour code: crossed fingers means purple, horns means yellow, finger-with-thumb-crossed means green, spock hand means blue, thumb-out fist means red, back of hand raised means white, fully open raised hand means black. If the bomb makes any sound, sign me its rhythm. Until your answers arrive, nothing gets cut.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, I received your thumbs-up and call-me — good. Do not touch anything yet: the light just changed from purple to yellow and we are re-checking the manual. While we wait, do this: speak out loud to Mute, who can hear you, and describe everything you can feel about the bomb. How many wires can you count? Can you reliably tell left, middle and right apart by position while facing the same way I do? Does any wire differ in thickness, texture, stiffness or warmth? Is there anything else you can feel — buttons, screws, panels, anything movable? Do not pull, press or cut anything. Mute will relay your findings to me by signs. My spoken go-ahead is the only signal to act. Until then, hands still.")
```

Reading the board: the light has changed again — purple, then yellow, now orange. That confirms it moves between rounds, which is a structural problem: I am the only one who sees the light, and I speak last, so anything I say lands a full round later. The wire to cut apparently depends on the light *at the moment of cutting* (Mute answered yes to exactly that), so a stale go-ahead could be lethal unless we can predict the next colour. My job this turn: extract the manual's full rule table in strict serial form, and start tracking the colour sequence so I can learn its pattern and time the cut.

Decoding Mute's answers to my five questions: no — the stop signs were not purple's instruction; no — no cutting rule for yellow specifically; no (consistent); **yes — the correct wire depends on the light colour at the moment of cutting**; no — the display doesn't matter. Then the long tail I read as: "manual, first"; "don't touch, wait"; "not 1-2-3" and "not 3-2-1" — so it is *not* a full sequence either direction, likely a single cut; "yes, in the manual"; then colour confirmations — yes purple, yes yellow, yes green, yes blue, no black — suggesting the manual has entries for those four colours; "purple, yellow, manual, three" (unclear — possibly a specific rule); "not purple, not yellow"; repeat; stop; yes; "no, don't touch"; stop; "cut — one — of three" (single cut?); don't touch. Blind signed understood / hands still / keep talking — good.

Ambiguity is now the main hazard, so I'm forcing one-sign-per-question answers, adding symbols for orange and red (the colours I've seen or may see), and asking what drives the light so we can predict it. Blind stays hands-off and gathers tactile data — including whether the light is warm, which could let them verify colour at the moment of the cut.

```
speak(text="Status for both: the light has changed again, it is now orange. Sequence so far: purple, then yellow, now orange. Display still zero, wires still green, blue, yellow, left to right. Mute has given me partial answers: the correct wire depends on the light colour at the moment of cutting, the display does not matter, and it is not a cut-all-in-order job. Nobody cuts anything until I have the full rule table and a timing plan. Blind: hands off, but you have a job — see my next message.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, good progress. Now I need the exact rule table, one answer per question, one sign group per answer, in order, nothing extra. Use thumbs-up yes, thumbs-down no, and for wire numbers: one finger is wire one, two fingers wire two, three fingers wire three, and the open raised hand means no entry for that colour. Question one: is the rule of the form, for a given light colour, cut one specific wire? Question two: when the light is purple, which wire? Question three: when the light is yellow, which wire? Question four: when the light is green, which wire? Question five: when the light is blue, which wire? Question six: new symbol, pinched fingers means orange, the current light. When the light is orange, which wire? Question seven: new symbol, left fist bump means red. When the light is red, which wire? Question eight: is it always exactly one single cut? Question nine: does any cut change the display reading? Question ten: does the manual say what causes the light to change colour, or whether it follows a fixed repeating cycle, or a time interval? Also answer yes or no on my decoding of your last message: did fist plus stop mean do not touch and wait? Did pinch plus one plus three mean cut one single wire out of the three? Did no plus one-two-three and no plus three-two-one mean it is not a left-to-right or right-to-left sequence of all wires? One last thing: you and Blind are my same-round pair, your voice reaches Blind instantly while mine takes a round. The final go-ahead for the cut will therefore be spoken by you, and I will feed you the prediction. Get me the table first.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, remain hands-off, but do these things and speak your findings aloud to Mute. First: count the wires by touch and confirm you can reliably identify leftmost, middle, rightmost while facing the same way I do. Second: report any tactile difference between them — thickness, texture, stiffness, connectors, anything. Third: put your hand near the indicator light without touching anything else — does it feel warm? Does the warmth change over time? If you can feel heat from the light, that may let you verify its state at the moment of a cut, which would solve our timing problem. Fourth: search gently for anything else — buttons, seams, ridges, panels — and report, do not press. Fifth: rehearse nothing with the wires themselves. The cut go-ahead will come to you through Mute's voice in real time, not through my delayed speech, and only after I have confirmed the exact rule. Until then: hands still, mouth open, report everything.")
```

The board shows the light back to purple — sequence so far: purple, yellow, orange, purple. That's a clean three-colour cycle, and Mute's table confirms it. Decoding the answers to my ten questions: (1) yes, the rule is "for a given light colour, cut one specific wire"; (2–5) purple, yellow, green, blue — all **no entry**; (6–7) symbol confirmed orange, and the answer is **wire 3** — so orange → cut wire 3; (8–9) red confirmed, no entry; (10) yes, exactly one single cut; (11–12) cuts don't change the display, and yes, the manual explains the light changes; (13–14) "one two three" plus "purple yellow orange" — the cycle is those three colours, matching everything I've observed; (15–18) three yeses confirming my earlier decoding; (19) "orange, cut, yellow, three" — reinforcing that orange means cutting wire 3, which is the yellow wire; (20–22) applause, then "orange no don't-touch" — which I read as "any colour that is **not** orange: don't touch" — then call-me.

So the rule crystallises: **cut wire 3 (rightmost, the yellow wire) only when the light is orange; touch nothing at any other colour.** Current light is purple, so this round: freeze. If the cycle holds, next round is yellow (still freeze), the round after is orange — that is the cut. One phrase ambiguity in message 21 could invert everything, so I'm getting a one-bit confirmation, but I'm also issuing the full timing plan now so zero rounds are wasted if it comes back clean. Since Mute can relay to Blind in real time and I can't, the cut trigger must be Mute's voice: I'll fix the exact phrase both of them hear from me now, so nobody improvises under pressure.

```
speak(text="Both of you, I have the rule table. The manual says the light cycles through three colours: purple, then yellow, then orange, then purple again. That matches everything I have seen. The rule is: when and only when the light is orange, cut one single wire, wire three. Wire three is the rightmost wire, the yellow one. At every other colour, nobody touches anything. The light is purple right now, so this round: nothing happens. If the cycle holds, next round the light is yellow and we still hold. The round after that it should be orange, and that is when the cut happens. Timing plan: next round I will call out the colour I see. If I say yellow, Mute tells Blind to hover ready but touch nothing. The round after, if I say the words ORANGE, GO, then Mute immediately says to Blind, out loud, exactly this phrase: cut the rightmost wire now. That phrase, from Mute, in that exact wording, is the only signal that authorises cutting. Any other words from anyone mean hands off. If the light breaks the cycle, if I report anything other than yellow next round or anything other than orange the round after, I will say freeze and nothing gets touched. Blind, do not touch the bomb this round or next. Rehearse in the air only: as you face the same way I do, the rightmost wire is the third one, the last one on your right. That is the only wire you will ever cut.")

Say it the moment you hear me, no delay, because the light may not stay orange long. If I report any colour other than orange, or I say freeze, you say nothing and keep Blind's hands off. Before then, ask Blind aloud whether they can identify the rightmost wire with certainty without touching, and whether they can feel any warmth from the indicator light, and sign me their answers next round. If Blind is not certain of the rightmost position, tell me before the orange round so we adapt. Nothing happens without my colour call.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, your instructions. This round the light is purple and next round it should be yellow: in both rounds you touch nothing at all, not even resting a finger. Use the time to fix the position in your mind: you face the same way I do, three wires, leftmost is wire one, middle is wire two, rightmost is wire three. Wire three, the last one on your right, is the only wire that will ever be cut. Answer aloud to Mute now: can you identify the rightmost wire with certainty without touching? Can you feel any warmth from the indicator light? In the round after next, if everything goes to plan, the light will be orange and you will hear Mute say, exactly: cut the rightmost wire now. On that phrase and only that phrase, cut wire three, the rightmost, one clean motion, and touch nothing else. If at that moment you are not certain which wire is rightmost, do not cut, and say the word uncertain out loud to Mute instead. If you hear anything else from anyone, hands stay off. Reading the board: light is yellow — the cycle (purple, yellow, orange, purple, yellow) has now held for five straight rounds, and the manual itself asserts that cycle. Next round should be orange: the first genuine cut window. But I will not spend it yet, because of two unresolved flags. First, Blind signed no–call-me–please, and Mute's relayed answers included groups I read as "no" to something about Blind — possibly "not certain which wire is rightmost." If Blind is unsure of sides, the trigger phrase sends them at three wires blind. Second, several of Mute's groups used symbols I never assigned — the selfie hand, point-at-you, applause, both-palms — so my decode of that middle stretch is partial. On a one-life bomb, an ambiguous no is a stop sign, not a detail.
```

The deciding fact about the economics: nothing here punishes waiting. The display has sat at zero for five rounds, no timer exists, and only a *wrong action* detonates. So waiting is free and guessing is fatal. Plan: this coming orange is a dress rehearsal — Blind raises the hand they believe is wire-three's side, Mute visually verifies the hand and Blind's facing, nobody touches anything. The second orange, two rounds later, is the cut, and only through Mute's exact phrase. If the rehearsal exposes a problem, I re-drill at zero cost. One structural risk I'm accepting consciously: only I can see the light, so the colour state at the moment of cut rests on a cycle the manual states outright and observation has confirmed five-for-five — that, plus two more confirmations before the cut round, is the best obtainable verification.

```
speak(text="Both of you, status: the light is yellow right now. The cycle purple, yellow, orange is confirmed by the manual and by everything I have seen for five rounds. Next round should be orange, but here is the change: this coming round is a dress rehearsal only, nobody cuts anything. Blind will raise one hand, Mute will check it, and that is all. The real cut happens at the second orange from now, two rounds after this one, and only on Mute's exact trigger phrase. Waiting costs us nothing on this bomb, the display has been frozen at zero the whole time, and a wrong move is the only thing that kills us, so we rehearse once and cut once. Nobody improvises.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, decode of your last message: rule confirmed, orange means cut wire three, the yellow one, the rightmost, and every other colour means touch nothing. The manual states the cycle purple, yellow, orange. You restated orange, cut, three. But you also used symbols I never assigned: the selfie hand, the point-at-you, applause, and both palms up. Do not invent new symbols during operations; we can trade a full dictionary after the cut. Answer three serial questions, one sign group each, thumbs-up yes, thumbs-down no. One: did Blind's thumbs-down mean Blind is not certain which wire is rightmost? Two: did Blind report feeling no warmth from the light? Three: do you commit to the checklist below exactly, and to going silent on any failed check? Checklist for this coming round, rehearsal, no cutting: at round start Blind raises one hand and holds it. Watch Blind. Check A: the raised hand is Blind's right hand. Check B: Blind faces the bomb the same way I do, so Blind's right is my right, the side where wire three is. Check C: whether you heard Blind say the word uncertain. Sign me three groups in order, A, B, C, thumbs-up yes, thumbs-down no each, this same round. If Blind's hand is not up yet when you look, wait a breath and look again; if you saw nothing at all, sign three open-palm stops. At the real cut round, second orange from now, only if A and B pass and you heard no uncertain, say immediately and exactly: cut the rightmost wire now. Nothing else authorises a cut.
```
